title: Individual productivity triples, but company delivery only shrinks from 20 days to 17
dek: AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weak link in the barrel isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform process and organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
why: A frontline CEO talks about building his own CEO AI, canceling weekly meetings, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and numbers are concrete, and the decision hub section in the second half is the most valuable.
who: CEOs, CTOs, and HR leaders at companies pushing AI adoption, especially managers trying to understand why individual productivity improved but the organization didn't get faster.
skip: The first 4 minutes of education-scenario setup can be fast-forwarded; go straight to the barrel weak-link case at 16:07.

points.h: Individual productivity triples, but delivery only speeds up by three days
points.body: NetEase did a study last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design draft to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled to quintupled their personal efficiency, some tenfold. But for features of the same scope, the entire process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of 20 staves, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product manager staves rise rapidly, but some staves aren't people — they're process — and they haven't improved at all. So AI adoption must clear three hurdles: cognition, applying it to individual short-range tasks, and transforming process and organization. The third is the hardest.

points.h: Cancel weekly meetings: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
points.body: Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. Weekly meetings usually serve three purposes: sync information, discover problems and opportunities, and make decisions. Previously they ran 2.5 hours a week, but the time spent for that meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepares materials layer by layer, and information sync itself isn't done well because no one listens attentively the whole time and may miss a sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agree on what information is needed, everyone fills in a template and stores it in the knowledge base, AI scans and integrates it into a focused, interactive HTML report where people can leave comments and follow up; an AI agent produces a preliminary list of problems and opportunities, which human brains confirm and supplement; problem-solving and decision-making become dedicated meetings.

points.h: SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
points.body: Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, it just changes form. AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may indeed die. Truly good SaaS that has entered a company's critical processes will only get better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. Previously humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future, large numbers of Agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, audit APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs. The call volume will far exceed the number and actions of humans, will increase enormously, and the more it's called, the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that the Service itself is critical enough within the enterprise.

points.h: Distill top salespeople into skills and distribute them to everyone
points.body: Bosses have two headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is too strong and what if they leave? Previously there was no solution, but now you can distill or extract the actions, scripts, and behaviors of good salespeople into skills. Two uses: distribute them to other salespeople for direct use; and have AI turn elite salespeople into teachers to train ordinary salespeople. What training should distill isn't the salesperson, it's the customer — take the customer interaction data the salesperson has had, such as calls, WeChat, emails, and let AI simulate various customers to train salespeople. Online sales are purely digital and on record; for offline sales, it's recommended or even required to equip them with a recording card. After a visit, while memory is fresh, record a two-to-three-minute voice note. Salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is for managing them), but they don't mind recording cards, because it's also useful for their own customer review.

points.h: Fewer middle managers, strong individuals lead Agent legions back to the front line
points.body: Ruan Liang judges that middle managers will become fewer, but not necessarily eliminated — rather, they'll go to the front line, and the front line can also lead a bunch of agents. Middle managers with management responsibilities will become fewer; elite individuals with strong skills will become more numerous. He gives the example of an engineering team: previously socialized division of labor split software development ever finer — frontend, backend, algorithm, test engineers; in the last half year it has clearly reverted to full-stack, everyone becoming full-end engineers. In the future, organizations will look more like a distributed structure: countless engineering capabilities are strong, a mother peak commands some engineering, and countless agents fight a battle. He imagines a future interview negotiation scenario: the candidate says I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, a summary of all my past experience and skills, and the premium the company pays might be some kind of OPC.

points.h: AI value formula: quality times time saved
points.body: Ruan Liang gives a formula referencing a paper: AI value = quality of AI completing the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at eight out of ten, AI also makes it at eight out of ten, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit time, and you can calculate ROI. Prioritize four types of tasks for AI: time-consuming, high-frequency, unavoidable, and tasks where different people produce roughly the same result. Once calculated, you can immediately decide whether to use AI. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Cloud, GPT) to prove the task can be done, solidify the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheaper ones can too.

points.h: Token consumption leads by a landslide, output also leads by a landslide
points.body: NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work tasks into points with work value. In the AI era, they found a group of people whose token consumption is astonishing, and whose work output and work value are also astonishing, forming a statistical pattern: people whose token consumption leads by a landslide are most likely building systems for themselves, saving their own work time and increasing thinking time, so their work quality and work results also lead by a landslide. Many bosses worry about waste from AI abuse; Ruan Liang's hot take is that truly excellent or elite people won't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through statistics they found elite colleagues don't waste. He also says small companies are more likely to fully embrace AI, because there are fewer organizational relationships, the boss uses it first, there are fewer layers, and the chain is shorter.

points.h: The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
points.body: Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base; what really matters is the historical decision processes and decision bases. This year NetEase preserved past decisions and included them in the knowledge base. Combining the two types of knowledge to train an agent or skill, then feeding back hundreds of original cases for the agent to judge, achieved accuracy over 90%. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater gave researchers and analysts agents they built themselves, precipitating decision processes and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater did better was making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a person adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment actions enter the next round of reinforcement, advancing with the times, equivalent to human-machine collaborative self-evolution.

quotes.text: Across our entire process, for software features of similar scope, from product requirement to launch, it only shortened from 20 days to 17 days.
The third and hardest hurdle to cross is actually transforming the process, your organization. Yes, once you transform the process, it inevitably means transforming the organization.
In a two-and-a-half-hour meeting, it's impossible to be that focused every second — that would take a god.
Middle managers with management responsibilities will become fewer, but elite individuals with strong skills should become more numerous.
If your token consumption leads by a landslide, your work quality and work results are also most likely leading by a landslide.
Sometimes it's not that the boss wants to push and can push — because many organizations have ten thousand reasons to make sure this thing doesn't get done.
It made the agent into a learnable, evolvable part.
